source.title: Uncovering a Universal Abstract Algorithm for Modular Addition in Neural Networks
source.authors: Gavin McCracken; Gabriela Moisescu-Pareja; Vincent Letourneau; Doina Precup; Jonathan Love

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, though PDF extraction has formatting artifacts in equations and figure/table text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether networks trained on modular addition converge on a shared algorithmic structure, using neuron, cluster, and network analyses rather than the original grokking trajectory measurement.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on internal structure across architectures and training conditions. It does not report training/test accuracy trajectories or delays; cited grokking results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study analyses trained MLPs and pizza/clock transformers on modular addition across seeds, hyperparameters, moduli and depth. It asks whether they share one algorithm, which bears directly on V6. It uses neuron fits, replacement tests and frequency counts rather than grokking trajectories, and reports no accuracy-over-time data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MLPs and transformers trained on modular addition universally implement one abstract algorithm, the approximate CRT. In it, neurons activate on approximate cosets despite differing low-level (clock/pizza) implementations. They add that the theory predicts, and experiments confirm, that networks with trainable embeddings or depth use O(log n) frequencies.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes learned neuron and network structure across architectures, rather than measuring grokking accuracy trajectories. It proposes and tests an approximate-coset/aCRT abstraction.
record.method_sensitivity: The representation forms depend on architecture and depth: deeper transformers can require order-two sinusoidal components in addition to order-one forms. The paper also reports variation with hyperparameters in frequency counts and learned mechanisms.
record.problems: The study does not quantify the proportion of hyperparameter-grid settings in which fitted-form replacement preserves accuracy. Its broad universality conclusion is supported by the authors' abstraction of different low-level implementations, rather than by showing identical circuits. Some additional frequency-counting results are explicitly described as approximate and potentially contaminated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested claim version were omitted. Results about embedding-weight distributions, noise, cluster ablations, and unrelated neuron properties were not included because they do not directly test whether networks share the identified algorithm.

untested.parts: No train/test accuracy trajectories, no delay measurements, and no variation of training-set size (90/10 split throughout).
Only final trained checkpoints are analysed. There is no time course of circuit formation or memorization removal.
No non-algorithmic data and no manipulation of initialization scale or weight norm.
No LLMs and no realistic data.
Weight decay is varied across the grid, but its effect on delay, critical dataset size or ungrokking is not measured.
Adam is always used, and there is no optimizer or floating-point control.

missing.what: The number of learned frequencies depends on architecture: one-hot 1-layer MLPs learn floor(n/2) frequencies, while added depth or a trainable embedding gives far fewer. Average counts over moduli 59–66 are reported. The authors say they do not know why.
missing.locator: Sec. 4.4, Fig. 4; Sec. 5.1; App. G.9.2 Figs. 40–41

missing.what: Frequency count grows as O(log n) across clocks, pizzas and MLPs over moduli up to about 5000, with high-R² log fits and 1 std error bars.
Across 100k seeds (mod 91 and mod 89), the learned frequencies are uniformly distributed, so specific frequencies differ per run. About 25% of runs contain 'fine-tuning' (multi-harmonic) neurons.
For n=66, all architectures prefer frequencies that give precise cosets. Clock models learn frequency-6 cosets in layer 1 in 1 of 4 cases.
Fig. 8: the share of layer-2 neurons best fit by order-one sinusoids in 2-layer transformers varies across the LR×WD grid.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The claim of universality depends on the chosen abstraction: the authors state that all sinusoidal neurons satisfy Theorem 4.4. The V6 support is therefore partly definitional, and researchers should weigh it against the measured variation in frequency counts, forms and harmonics. Only fully trained models are studied, with Adam and L2 throughout. No grokking dynamics are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No training-accuracy/test-accuracy trajectory, post-overfitting delay, or training-set-size versus optimization-delay test.
No time-course of circuit formation or memorizing-component removal, and no test of whether continuous progress measures anticipate a generalization jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets and no controlled test of initialization scale, weight norm, or a lazy-to-rich transition as a cause of delays.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
L2 regularization is used, but the study does not test an efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
Tests shared structure at the abstract aCRT level, not whether all networks use identical neuron-level implementations or converge to the same solution in every architecture and setting.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

rows.subject: Networks trained on modular addition across architectures (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze neuron activations and representational structure using the simple-neuron and approximate-coset framework.

conditions.value: MLPs and transformers; varied hyperparameters, seeds, moduli, and depth

rows.measure: Whether the learned structures fit the proposed abstract aCRT
rows.value: The authors report that layer 1 uses only simple neurons, other layers also use them, and all architectures are well abstracted by approximate cosets.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the architectures and conditions discussed; the study does not provide a single numerical rate for this result.
rows.check: This is the authors' summary claim (Sec. 4.4, 5) rather than a measured value. It rests on R2–R3 and the frequency analyses, so it should not count as independent evidence.

source_check.problem: Accurate authors' summary, but not an independent measured result beyond the fits, replacements and frequency analyses.

rows.subject: MLP models (aggregate; one-hot and embedding variants, 1–4 hidden layers)
rows.size_stated: 1024 neurons in every layer; embedding matrix has 128 features where used
rows.operation_detail: Fit simple-neuron sinusoidal forms to activations and test replacement of neurons with the fitted forms.

conditions.value: learning rates and weight decays varied

rows.measure: Test accuracy after replacing neurons with fitted forms
rows.value: The text reports that fitted forms maintain 100% test accuracy; Figure 6 shows a large volume of successful cases across the hyperparameter grid.
rows.locator: Section 4.4, Figure 6; experimental details in E.6
rows.note: The paper does not state the fraction of grid conditions that succeed; the text describes a large volume of green checkmarks, not all conditions.
rows.check: The state is right. Clarify the value: each grid cell has 10 seeds, and a cell is purple if any seed loses 100% accuracy after replacement. Fig. 6 shows mostly green cells but not all, and no fraction is given. The numbers_found entry '1/1' is spurious.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.4, depth discussion and Figure 6 caption; Appendix E.6.
source_check.problem: The text supports successful 100% replacements and many green checkmarks; actual grid contents and the success proportion are unavailable in this extraction.

rows.subject: Pizza and clock transformer models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 1024 neurons in every layer; embedding matrix has 128 features
rows.operation_detail: Fit order-one and order-two sinusoidal forms to neuron activations and test replacement using those forms.

conditions.value: learning rates and weight decays varied

rows.measure: Test accuracy after replacement with fitted forms
rows.value: The text reports that the fitted forms maintain 100% accuracy in many cases; Figure 7 shows a large volume of successful cases.
rows.locator: Section 4.4, Figures 7–8; experimental details in E.7–E.8
rows.note: Deeper transformers require order-two forms as well as order-one forms; the text does not give the fraction of successful configurations.
rows.check: Order-one fits keep accuracy only in layer 1. Later transformer layers need order-two cos(f(a+b)) terms or mixtures of the two. Fig. 8 shows that nearly 100% order-one neurons in layer 2 occurs in 'very little volume' of the grid. The numbers_found entry '1/1' is spurious.

source_check.correct: Figure 7 replacement experiments use 1024 neurons per layer. Figure 8 uses two layers with 2048 neurons per layer. Later transformer layers require first-order and second-order terms or their mixtures.
source_check.problem: The aggregate 1024-neuron specification incorrectly includes Figure 8.

rows.subject: MLPs, pizza transformers, and clock transformers (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the algorithmic structures inferred from different architectures and circuit realizations.
rows.value: The authors report differing low-level mechanisms, including clock and pizza circuits, but interpret them as realizations of a common approximate CRT template.
rows.note: Supports shared structure at the authors' abstract level, while explicitly distinguishing it from identical circuit-level mechanisms.
rows.check: The clock/pizza divergence comes from cited prior work (Zhong et al.), which the study reinterprets. The study's own evidence here is qualitative (Figs. 1, 44–46), showing remapped pizza and clock neurons look like simple neurons. Commonality holds only at the abstract-template level.

source_check.locator_found: Abstract; Sections 2, 4.2 and 5; Appendix A.1; Appendix G.10.1–G.10.2.
source_check.problem: Commonality concerns an abstract network-level template; the qualitative clock/pizza examples reuse prior checkpoints and do not establish identical circuits.

relationships.condition: Abstract-algorithm level, across 1–4 layer MLPs (one-hot and embedded) and pizza/clock transformers, LR×WD grids with 10 seeds, and prime and composite moduli
relationships.reason: Layer-1 neurons fit as simple sinusoids, and replacing neurons with fitted forms keeps 100% accuracy across most grid cells. Remapped pizza and clock neurons look alike, which the authors read as one aCRT template (R1, R2, R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Replacing first-layer neurons with fitted sinusoids preserved 100% accuracy in most tested settings, and similar remapped Pizza and Clock neurons motivated a shared aCRT template.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Abstract-algorithm level, across 1–4 layer MLPs (one-hot and embedded) and pizza/clock transformers, LR×WD grids with 10 seeds, and prime and composite moduli
source_check.reason: R1–R4 support common aCRT structure at the authors' abstraction level. Successful replacements retain 100% accuracy; the text does not quantify a majority of successful cells. Appendix E.4 specifically documents one-hot MLP depths 1–4 and an embedded one-hidden-layer MLP.

relationships.condition: Neuron and circuit level, and the dependence on architecture, depth and hyperparameters
relationships.reason: Deeper transformers need order-two forms, and the share of order-one neurons varies across the grid. Replacement fails in some grid cells. Frequency counts shift from floor(n/2) to O(log n) with depth or embedding (text, Fig. 4). Identity therefore holds only under a loose abstraction that, by the authors' account, any sinusoidal neuron satisfies (R2, R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Deeper transformers required order-two forms, order-one neuron prevalence varied, fitted-neuron replacement sometimes failed, and depth or embeddings shifted the number of frequencies from floor(n/2) to O(log n).

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Neuron and circuit level, and the dependence on architecture, depth and hyperparameters
source_check.reason: R2–R4 qualify circuit-level identity: transformer fitting forms depend on depth and hyperparameters, and shared aCRT structure accommodates lower-level differences. These explicit qualifications suffice without assuming unverified grid failures.

tranche.reason: Neuron fits, fitted-form replacements and frequency analyses address algorithm identity across training conditions using a different method.

source_check.notes: Figures 6–8 lack their grid contents in the text extraction, preventing verification of particular failed cells or a majority success claim. Supplementary code is reported; the abstract aCRT interpretation does not establish identical circuits or grokking trajectories.

statements.correction: Section 4.4: successful fitted replacements retain 100% test accuracy; captions describe many green checkmarks without a success fraction. Appendix E.2: figure-generation code is reported in supplementary materials; other experimental code filenames are provided.
statements.problem: The 100% replacement accuracy is supported, but a majority of grid cells cannot be verified from the extracted captions. The claim of no reported code contradicts Appendix E.2.

statements.correction: Section 4.4: first-order forms alone are insufficient in later transformer layers; fits include second-order terms and mixtures. Appendices E.6–E.8 define a purple cell as at least one seed losing 100% accuracy, but do not enumerate such cells.
statements.problem: Depth-dependent fitted forms are supported. Actual failures of the full fitted-form replacement in particular grid cells cannot be confirmed because grid contents are missing.

statements.correction: Appendix A.1: common network-level aCRT structure can coexist with differing circuit-level mechanisms. Appendix D: embedding distributions vary with batch size without identified significant differences in core learned structures.
statements.problem: The abstraction-level distinction is supported, but this text does not explicitly judge symmetric feature selection insufficient or report a comparison against output-gradient diagnostics.

statements.correction: Supplementary figure-generation code is explicitly reported in Appendix E.2. Successful replacements preserve 100% accuracy; the successful-grid proportion is unstated. Later transformer layers use richer sinusoidal forms. The paper reports noise and neuron-ablation experiments in Appendix G.8.
statements.problem: No reported code is incorrect. Some full-replacement failures cannot be verified from the missing grids; later-layer fitting qualifications and successful 100% replacements are supported.
